{{short description|Integral transform}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[integral geometry]], the '''Funk transform''' (also known as '''Minkowski–Funk transform''', '''Funk–Radon transform''' or '''spherical Radon transform''') is an [[integral transform]] defined by integrating a [[function (mathematics)|function]] on [[great circle]]s of the [[sphere]].  It was introduced by [[Paul Funk]] in 1911, based on the work of {{harvtxt|Minkowski|1904}}.  It is closely related to the [[Radon transform]].  The original motivation for studying the Funk transform was to describe [[Zoll surface|Zoll metrics]] on the sphere.

== Definition ==
The Funk transform is defined as follows.  Let ''&fnof;'' be a [[continuous function]] on the [[sphere|d-1-sphere]] '''S'''<sup>d-1</sup> in '''R'''<sup>d</sup>.  Then, for a [[unit vector]] '''x''', let

:<math>Ff(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{u}\in C(\mathbf{x})} f(\mathbf{u})\,ds(\mathbf{u})</math>

where the integral is carried out with respect to the arclength ''ds'' of the great circle ''C''('''x''') consisting of all unit vectors perpendicular to '''x''':

:<math>C(\mathbf{x}) = \{\mathbf{u}\in S^{d-1}\mid \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}=0\}.</math>

== Inversion ==
The Funk transform annihilates all [[odd function]]s, and so it is natural to confine attention to the case when ''&fnof;'' is even.  In that case, the Funk transform takes even (continuous) functions to even continuous functions, and is furthermore invertible.

=== Spherical harmonics ===
Every [[square-integrable function]] <math>f\in L^2 (S^2)</math> on the sphere can be decomposed into [[spherical harmonics]] <math>Y_n^k</math>

:<math>f = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{k=-n}^n \hat f (n,k) Y_n^k.</math>

Then the Funk transform of ''f'' reads

:<math>F f = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{k=-n}^n P_n(0) \hat f (n,k) Y_n^k</math>

where <math>P_{2n+1}(0)=0</math> for odd values and 
:<math>P_{2n}(0) = (-1)^n\, \frac{1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdots 2n-1}{2\cdot 4\cdot 6 \cdots 2n}
= (-1)^n\, \frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2n)!!}</math> 
for even values. This result was shown by {{harvtxt|Funk|1913}}.

=== Helgason's inversion formula ===
Another inversion formula is due to {{harvtxt|Helgason|1999}}.
As with the Radon transform, the inversion formula relies on the dual transform ''F''* defined by

:<math>(F^*f)(p,\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2\pi\cos p}\int_{\|\mathbf{u}\|=1,\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{u}=\sin p} f(\mathbf{u})\,|d\mathbf{u}|.</math>

This is the average value of the circle function ''&fnof;'' over circles of arc distance ''p'' from the point '''x'''.  The inverse transform is given by

:<math>f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\left\{\frac{d}{du}\int_0^u F^*(Ff)(\cos^{-1}v,\mathbf{x})v(u^2-v^2)^{-1/2}\,dv\right\}_{u=1}.</math>

== Generalization ==
The classical formulation is invariant under the [[rotation group SO(3)]].  It is also possible to formulate the Funk transform in a manner that makes it invariant under the [[special linear group]] SL(3,'''R''')  {{harv|Bailey|Eastwood|Gover|Mason|2003}}.  Suppose that ''&fnof;'' is a [[homogeneous function]] of degree &minus;2 on '''R'''<sup>3</sup>.  Then, for [[linear independence|linearly independent]] vectors '''x''' and '''y''', define a function φ by the [[line integral]]

:<math>\varphi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint f(u\mathbf{x} + v\mathbf{y})(u\,dv-v\,du)</math>

taken over a simple closed curve encircling the origin once.  The [[differential form]]

:<math>f(u\mathbf{x} + v\mathbf{y})(u\,dv-v\,du)</math>

is [[closed and exact differential forms|closed]], which follows by the homogeneity of ''&fnof;''.  By a [[integration by substitution|change of variables]], φ satisfies

:<math>\phi(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y},c\mathbf{x}+d\mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{|ad-bc|}\phi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),</math>

and so gives a homogeneous function of degree &minus;1 on the [[exterior algebra|exterior square]] of '''R'''<sup>3</sup>,

:<math>Ff(\mathbf{x}\wedge\mathbf{y}) = \phi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).</math>

The function ''F&fnof;''&nbsp;:&nbsp;Λ<sup>2</sup>'''R'''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' agrees with the Funk transform when ''&fnof;'' is the degree &minus;2 homogeneous extension of a function on the sphere and the projective space associated to Λ<sup>2</sup>'''R'''<sup>3</sup> is identified with the space of all circles on the sphere.  Alternatively, Λ<sup>2</sup>'''R'''<sup>3</sup> can be identified with '''R'''<sup>3</sup> in an SL(3,'''R''')-invariant manner, and so the Funk transform ''F'' maps smooth even homogeneous functions of degree &minus;2 on '''R'''<sup>3</sup>\{0} to smooth even homogeneous functions of degree &minus;1 on '''R'''<sup>3</sup>\{0}.

== Applications ==
The Funk-Radon transform is used in the Q-Ball method for [[Diffusion MRI]] introduced by {{harvtxt|Tuch|2004}}.
It is also related to [[intersection body|intersection bodies]] in convex geometry. 
Let <math>K\subset \mathbb R^d</math> be a [[star body]] with radial function <math>\rho_K(\boldsymbol x)=\max\{t:t\boldsymbol x\in K\},</math> <math>x\in S^{d-1}</math>.
Then the intersection body ''IK'' of ''K'' has the radial function <math>\rho_{IK}=F\rho_K</math> {{harv|Gardner|2006|p=305}}.
